abstract: Leaf mesophyll architecture has a great impact on plant functions, including photosynthesis. Yet, understanding the principles governing growth, stability, and interspecific variation of leaf mesophyll architecture remains elusive. Here, we develop a computational framework based on stochastic space tessellation to simulate two-dimensional paradermal slices of leaf spongy mesophyll across 40 vascular plant species using three data-derived parameters: leaf porosity, cell arm length, and cell arm diameter. The framework successfully reconstructs leaf slices while preserving six biological, topological, and cell-level traits, with one- to three-armed cell geometries generally outperforming circular cells. Importantly, we further develop a theoretical model based on stochastic geometry that closely agrees with the simulations and reveals that leaf porosity strongly influences cell wall construction cost, while cell-arm statistics shape this relationship. Our parsimoniously parameterized model provides a basis for optimizing leaf architecture to maximize carbon dioxide uptake while minimizing cell wall construction costs.
